name: Nepal
blurb: The Shah kings, from Gorkha's conqueror to the 2008 republic
dateConvention: Nepal's official calendar is the Vikram Samvat; the deck gives every date in the Gregorian calendar. From 1846 to 1951 the hereditary Rana prime ministers held real power while the Shah kings reigned as figureheads.
epilogue: On 28 May 2008 Nepal's Constituent Assembly abolished the monarchy and declared a federal democratic republic. Gyanendra left the palace that June and lives on in Nepal as a private citizen.

reigns.tagline: The hill king who swallowed the Kathmandu valley
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of King Nara Bhupal Shah of Gorkha
reigns.previously: Three rich Malla kingdoms share one valley. A hill state watches.
paragraphs: In the 1740s the Kathmandu valley was a jewel box split three ways. Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur were rich Newar cities, each with its own Malla king, and they spent their energy feuding. A few days' march to the west sat Gorkha, a poor hill kingdom with hungry soldiers. In 1743 a young man of about 20 became its king. Prithvi Narayan Shah wanted the valley, and he was patient enough to starve it.

He seized the hill forts and passes around the valley and choked its trade with Tibet and India. Kirtipur, a hilltop town by Patan, beat him off twice and fell at last to a third attack. Then, on 25 September 1768, while Kathmandu was busy celebrating the Indra Jatra festival, his troops walked in. Its king fled to Patan, which fell within days. Bhaktapur fell in 1769. Prithvi Narayan made Kathmandu his capital. This was the birth of the Kingdom of Nepal.

He threw out the Capuchin friars, wary of Europeans who arrived as priests and stayed as conquerors. Late in life he dictated advice that his followers wrote down as the Dibya Upadesh. Nepal, he said, was a yam between two boulders, China and British India, and must tread carefully. (Nepali sources date all of this in the Vikram Samvat calendar, about 57 years ahead.) He died at Nuwakot in January 1775, his conquests still rolling on.

claims.text: After Kirtipur fell, the conquerors cut off the noses and lips of its men.
claims.note: The story comes from the Capuchin friar Giuseppe, who was in the valley at the time. Later writers repeat it, but the numbers vary wildly.

claims.text: Prithvi Narayan called Nepal 'a yam between two boulders'.
claims.note: The saying is in the Dibya Upadesh, attributed to him. It was written down by his followers, so the wording is theirs.

claims.text: He sat on Kathmandu's throne during Indra Jatra and took the blessing meant for its own king.
claims.note: A popular tale told about the night the city fell. The capture during the festival is well attested; the throne scene is later colour.

reigns.hook: The conqueror is dead and his eldest son, Pratap Singh, takes the throne. But Pratap's younger brother, Bahadur Shah, is clever, ambitious and very close to the army.

reigns.tagline: Two short years on a brand-new throne
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Eldest son of Prithvi Narayan Shah
reigns.previously: Prithvi Narayan has conquered the valley and died at Nuwakot.
paragraphs: Pratap Singh Shah inherited a kingdom that was barely ten years old and still hungry. His father's generals wanted to keep marching. Pratap mostly kept them home. His reign was short and inward-looking, spent holding together a court full of proud captains, priests and relatives who had all helped win the valley and all wanted a reward.

The sharpest quarrel was inside the family. His younger brother Bahadur Shah had real talent and real friends, and that made him dangerous. Pratap had him put under house arrest, and Bahadur ended up living in exile outside the kingdom. Then in November 1777 Pratap died, still in his twenties. He left behind a son, Rana Bahadur, who was two years old. A toddler now sat on the throne of a warrior state, and everyone at court began working out who would rule in his name.

claims.text: Bahadur Shah was locked up and pushed out because he was plotting against his brother.
claims.note: Pratap had him held at Nuwakot, reportedly on a royal adviser's urging. Plotting charges were a common court weapon, and historians such as Stiller treat this one as faction politics.

claims.text: Pratap Singh paused his father's conquests.
claims.note: Standard histories agree that expansion stalled in his brief reign and picked up again under the regents who followed.

reigns.hook: Nepal has a two-year-old king. His mother and his exiled uncle Bahadur Shah both want to rule for him. Whoever wins gets an army that is itching to march again.

reigns.tagline: The wild king who quit, came back and was stabbed
reigns.previously: Pratap Singh dies after two years, leaving a two-year-old son.
paragraphs: For years others ruled for Rana Bahadur. First his mother, Queen Rajendra Lakshmi, then his uncle Bahadur Shah, back from exile. Bahadur was a gifted soldier. His armies pushed west, taking Kumaon in 1790. Then Nepal raided Tibet, and in 1792 a Qing Chinese army marched across the Himalaya to within a few days of Kathmandu. Nepal made peace at Betrawati and promised tribute to Beijing. Once grown, Rana Bahadur grabbed power and threw his uncle in jail, where he died in 1797.

Rana Bahadur was erratic and violent. He fell for Kantavati, a Brahmin widow, and married her, a scandal at court. When she fell gravely ill he abdicated, in March 1799, for her baby son, and became a swami, a holy man. After she died he raged at the gods who had failed to save her. He later moved to Varanasi in India. Bored of holiness, he returned in 1804 and took charge as chief minister.

It did not last. In April 1806 his half-brother Sher Bahadur stabbed him to death in Kathmandu. Courtiers cut down the killer on the spot. What followed was a bloodbath: dozens of nobles were executed at Bhandarkhal, by the palace, in the purge that cleared the way for a rising officer named Bhimsen Thapa.

claims.text: After Kantavati died, Rana Bahadur had temples defiled and images of gods smashed.
claims.note: Widely told and in keeping with his reputation, but the details vary between accounts. Even her illness is told differently: smallpox in many retellings, tuberculosis in others.

claims.text: A Chinese army came within striking distance of Kathmandu in 1792.
claims.note: Qing and Nepali records agree the army reached the Nuwakot area before the Treaty of Betrawati.

claims.text: Sher Bahadur's killer was Bal Narsingh Kunwar, father of the future strongman Jung Bahadur.
claims.note: Recorded in standard histories of the period. Some accounts say another courtier, Bam Shah, struck too.

reigns.hook: Rana Bahadur has left the throne to a baby, Girvan Yuddha. Real power will soon pass to Bhimsen Thapa, and Nepal is about to collide with the East India Company.

reigns.tagline: A child king, a giant kingdom and a war with Britain
reigns.previously: Rana Bahadur quits the throne for a swami's robe in Varanasi.
paragraphs: Girvan Yuddha was a baby king, and he never really ruled. After his father's murder in 1806, Bhimsen Thapa became mukhtiyar, chief minister, and ran Nepal for three decades. Some of Rana Bahadur's widows were burned on his pyre in the old rite of sati. Bhimsen kept the armies marching, and Nepal reached its greatest size stretching from the Sutlej river in the west to the Teesta in the east.

That pushed Nepal up against the East India Company. Border fights turned into war in 1814. At Nalapani, Balbhadra Kunwar's few hundred defenders held a hill fort for a month against a much larger British force, and the British general Rollo Gillespie was killed in the first assault. In the west Amar Singh Thapa fought hard, but General David Ochterlony outmanoeuvred him and forced his surrender.

The Treaty of Sugauli, signed in December 1815 and ratified in March 1816, cost Nepal about a third of its land and put a British Resident in Kathmandu. The British were so impressed by their enemies that they started recruiting them. The Gurkha regiments were born. Then, in November 1816, the 19-year-old king caught smallpox and died.

claims.text: Several of Rana Bahadur's queens and servant women burned on his pyre.
claims.note: That sati took place is recorded, but sources disagree on how many women died.

claims.text: The British began recruiting Gurkha soldiers during and right after this war.
claims.note: Company records show the first Gurkha battalions raised in 1815. The tradition continues in the British Army today.

claims.text: Nalapani's defenders walked out only when their water ran out.
claims.note: British accounts of the siege say the garrison broke out after the British cut off its water.

reigns.hook: The young king is dead of smallpox. His son Rajendra is two. Bhimsen Thapa means to keep running the country, but his enemies are already counting the years.

reigns.tagline: The weak king who lost his crown in a night of knives
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Girvan Yuddha Bikram Shah
reigns.previously: The young king dies of smallpox. Bhimsen Thapa still holds the reins.
paragraphs: Rajendra was two when he became king, and Bhimsen Thapa ruled for another twenty years. In 1837 the king's baby son died, and Bhimsen was accused of having him poisoned. He fell from power, and in 1839, back in prison, he killed himself. Nepal then slid into a feud between the Thapas and the rival Pande clan, with Rajendra's two queens and his violent son Surendra all pulling in different directions.

On the night of 14 September 1846 Gagan Singh, the favourite of Rajendra's junior queen, Rajya Lakshmi, was murdered. The queen summoned the nobles to the Kot, the palace armoury, to find the killer. Swords came out, and when it was over dozens of courtiers lay dead, many cut down by the men of an officer named Jung Bahadur Kunwar. Jung Bahadur came out of the Kot as prime minister.

Weeks later the queen was caught in a plot against him and sent into exile in India, and Rajendra went with her. In May 1847 Jung Bahadur declared him deposed and put his son Surendra on the throne. That summer Rajendra tried to fight his way back with an armed band, was beaten at Alau and captured. He lived on, a prisoner in Bhaktapur, until 1881.

claims.text: Around 30 to 40 nobles were killed in the Kot massacre.
claims.note: Contemporary and later accounts give different totals. Who struck first is also argued over.

claims.text: Bhimsen Thapa cut his own throat in prison in 1839.
claims.note: Reported by the British Resident and repeated by all standard histories.

claims.text: Jung Bahadur had planned the Kot massacre in advance.
claims.note: His enemies said so. His family's biography paints him as reacting to danger. Historians such as Whelpton weigh both.

reigns.hook: Rajendra is gone. Jung Bahadur crowns Surendra, a prince with a nasty reputation, and then makes sure the new king will never hold any real power at all.

reigns.tagline: The king in a gilded cage while the Ranas ruled
reigns.previously: After the Kot massacre, Rajendra is deposed and held in Bhaktapur.
paragraphs: Surendra was king, but Jung Bahadur ran Nepal. He took the grand name Rana and made the prime minister's job hereditary in his family, passing from brother to brother. In 1856 a royal decree made him Maharaja of Kaski and Lamjung, with powers over the king. The Shah kings kept their thrones and their palace and lost everything else. This was the Rana regime, and it lasted a century.

Jung Bahadur was a showman. In 1850 he sailed to Britain, met Queen Victoria, and toured France too. Home again, he issued the Muluki Ain (1854), Nepal's first national law code. He fought Tibet in 1855–56. When India rose against British rule in 1857, he led Nepali troops to help crush the rebellion, and Britain paid him back with a strip of the western Terai lowlands that Nepal had lost at Sugauli.

Surendra stayed in the palace. Tales of his cruelty spread. Jung Bahadur died in 1877, and his brother Ranodip Singh took over. Surendra's son Trailokya died before him, so when the king died in May 1881, the crown passed to a five-year-old grandson.

claims.text: Jung Bahadur was the first Nepali ruler to cross the sea.
claims.note: Often said, since crossing 'the black water' was taboo for high-caste Hindus. Hard to prove nobody earlier went.

claims.text: Surendra made courtiers jump into wells to see if they survived.
claims.note: The stories come mostly from Rana-era writers, who had every reason to make the king look unfit to rule.

claims.text: A royal decree of 1856 gave Jung Bahadur powers over the king.
claims.note: The sanad of 1856 is documented. It made him Maharaja of Kaski and Lamjung.

reigns.hook: The new king is five. His Rana prime minister is ageing, and Jung Bahadur's ambitious nephews, the Shumsher brothers, are growing impatient.

reigns.tagline: Thirty years on the throne, and not a day in charge
reigns.previously: Surendra dies. His son died first, so the crown skips a generation.
paragraphs: Prithvi Bir Bikram Shah was five when he was crowned, and he never ruled. The question in Kathmandu was which Rana did. In November 1885 the Shumsher brothers, sons of Jung Bahadur's youngest brother, shot their uncle, Prime Minister Ranodip Singh, in his palace. Jung Bahadur's eldest son, Jagat Jung, was killed too, and others of his family fled to India. From now on the Shumsher line would hold the job.

Bir Shumsher ruled as prime minister until 1901. His brother Dev lasted only a few months: he was a reformer who started the newspaper Gorkhapatra, and his brothers pushed him out. The next one, Chandra Shumsher, ran Nepal for almost thirty years. He kept Britain close. Gurkha recruiting went on, and when Britain sent Francis Younghusband into Tibet in 1903–04, Chandra helped supply it.

All this time the king stayed in his palace. He signed what he was given. Prithvi Bir died in December 1911, aged 36. His son Tribhuvan was five, and the Ranas were happy to have another child on the throne.

claims.text: The Shumsher brothers murdered their uncle Ranodip Singh in 1885 and seized power.
claims.note: The coup is fully documented and was well known to the British Resident at the time.

claims.text: Dev Shumsher was ousted because his reforms alarmed his brothers.
claims.note: That is the usual explanation. Others stress plain rivalry with Chandra.

reigns.hook: A five-year-old called Tribhuvan is crowned. Chandra Shumsher is in his prime. Nobody expects the boy to be the king who finally ends Rana rule.

reigns.tagline: The prisoner king who escaped and broke the Ranas
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Prithvi Bir Bikram Shah
reigns.previously: Prithvi Bir dies after 30 years as a figurehead.
paragraphs: Tribhuvan grew up a puppet. Chandra Shumsher ran Nepal and won a prize: in 1923 a treaty with Britain recognised Nepal's full independence. In 1924 he announced the end of slavery. Gurkhas fought for Britain in both world wars. But Tribhuvan was quietly listening to the opposition. In 1941 the Ranas executed four activists, now honoured as Nepal's martyrs.

On 6 November 1950 the king and his family drove into the Indian embassy and asked for refuge. Days later they flew to Delhi. The Ranas crowned his three-year-old grandson Gyanendra in his place, but India refused to recognise the boy. The Nepali Congress launched an armed rising, and India pushed a deal. On 7 January 1951 Tribhuvan was restored as king.

He flew home in February 1951 and on 18 February proclaimed a new democratic order. Nepal still marks the date (7 Falgun) as Democracy Day. The last Rana prime minister, Mohan Shumsher, resigned in November 1951. Governments came and went fast. In 1953 Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary climbed Everest. Tribhuvan fell ill and died in Zürich in March 1955.

claims.text: The Ranas crowned Tribhuvan's three-year-old grandson Gyanendra king in 1950.
claims.note: Done on 7 November 1950. India refused to recognise him, and Tribhuvan was restored two months later.

claims.text: Tribhuvan's escape began with what looked like a family picnic outing.
claims.note: Popular retellings say the royal party left the palace on the pretext of a hunt or picnic. Accounts differ on the cover story.

claims.text: Slavery in Nepal was abolished under Chandra Shumsher.
claims.note: Announced in 1924, with owners compensated. Standard histories agree.

reigns.hook: The king who beat the Ranas is dead. His son Mahendra inherits a young democracy, and he is far from sure he likes it.

reigns.previously: King Tribhuvan flees to the Indian embassy.
paragraphs: In November 1950 King Tribhuvan fled to the Indian embassy to escape the Rana prime ministers who had ruled Nepal for a century. The Ranas crowned his three-year-old grandson Gyanendra instead.
India and Britain refused to recognise the boy. Two months later the Ranas gave in, Tribhuvan returned, and the Rana regime ended. Gyanendra became king again in 2001.
reigns.hook: Tribhuvan returns in triumph, and the Rana era is over.

review.notes: Short card added from the completeness audit; checked only against Wikipedia.

reigns.tagline: The king who let democracy in, then shut it out
reigns.previously: Tribhuvan, who broke the Ranas, dies in a Zürich hospital.
paragraphs: Mahendra came to the throne with a clear idea of who should rule Nepal: himself. Nepal joined the United Nations in December 1955, and he was crowned in 1956. He allowed the first general election in 1959, and the Nepali Congress won a big majority. Its leader, B. P. Koirala, became prime minister and started on land and tax reforms that worried landowners.

On 15 December 1960 Mahendra struck. He dismissed the government, dissolved parliament and had Koirala arrested. Koirala spent years in jail without trial. Parties were banned. The 1962 constitution set up the 'partyless' Panchayat system: councils from village to national level, with the king firmly in control. Supporters saw a firm hand that held a fragile country together. Opponents saw a royal dictatorship.

He pushed land reform, began the long East–West Highway and played the giants off against each other. China helped build the road from Kathmandu to the Tibetan border at Kodari, which made India nervous. In January 1972 he died of a heart attack at Bharatpur, in the lowlands.

claims.text: Koirala was held for about eight years without trial.
claims.note: He was arrested in December 1960 and released in 1968. Widely documented.

claims.text: The 1960 takeover had Indian approval in advance.
claims.note: Some at the time suspected it. Delhi publicly criticised the coup, and historians find no clear evidence of a green light.

reigns.hook: Mahendra is dead. His son Birendra, educated at Eton and Harvard, takes the throne and inherits the Panchayat system. Change is coming, and it will not ask permission.

reigns.tagline: The king who gave way to democracy
reigns.previously: Mahendra, who ruled without parties, dies of a heart attack.
paragraphs: Birendra had studied at Eton, in Tokyo and at Harvard, and was crowned in 1975. He proposed that Nepal be declared a 'Zone of Peace' between India and China. He kept his father's Panchayat system, but protests in 1979 forced a referendum, and in 1980 voters kept it by a narrow margin. In 1989–90 India squeezed Nepal with a trade blockade. Then in 1990 the People's Movement filled the streets.

Birendra gave way. He lifted the ban on parties, and the 1990 constitution made him a constitutional monarch. Many Nepalis respected him for it. Democracy was messy, though. In 1996 the Maoists launched an armed insurgency in the hills.

On the evening of 1 June 2001 the royal family met for a dinner at Narayanhiti Palace. Nine of them were shot dead, among them the king, Queen Aishwarya, and their younger children, Nirajan and Shruti. An official inquiry, led by the Chief Justice and the Speaker of parliament, found that Crown Prince Dipendra, drunk and armed, had fired the shots and then shot himself.

claims.text: Voters kept the Panchayat system in the 1980 referendum.
claims.note: Official results gave about 55 per cent for the Panchayat system and 45 per cent for multiparty rule.

claims.text: Dipendra's anger over his parents' opposition to his choice of bride was the motive.
claims.note: This was the motive most widely reported. The inquiry described the events; the reason remains a matter of reports and inference.

claims.text: The official account of the massacre is complete and correct.
claims.note: Many Nepalis never accepted the inquiry's finding, which was produced in two weeks, and doubts about the official account persist.

reigns.hook: Under the law of succession, the crown passes to the heir. Dipendra is in hospital with a gunshot wound to the head, in a coma.

reigns.tagline: Three days as king, never conscious
reigns.cameToPower: Declared king while in a coma
reigns.previously: King Birendra and eight of his family are shot dead at the palace.
paragraphs: Dipendra had been crown prince since 1972. He went to Eton and was known as a keen soldier with a passion for guns. On 2 June 2001, the day after the killings, the Council of State declared him king. He was lying in a military hospital in a coma with a gunshot wound to the head. His uncle Gyanendra was named regent.
He was the man the official inquiry would name as the killer. He never regained consciousness. He died on 4 June 2001, the tenth death from that night. He had been king for three days.

claims.text: Dipendra was declared king while in a coma.
claims.note: The Council of State's decision of 2 June 2001 was public, with Gyanendra as regent.

claims.text: The inquiry found that Dipendra did the shooting and then shot himself.
claims.note: That is the finding of the official High-Level Committee report of June 2001. Many Nepalis doubted it, as the previous card notes.

reigns.hook: Dipendra is dead. The crown passes to Birendra's brother Gyanendra, who has worn it once before, as a small child in 1950.

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Brother of Birendra; uncle of Dipendra
reigns.previously: Dipendra, declared king in a coma, dies after three days.
paragraphs: Gyanendra had been made king once before, in 1950, when he was three and the Ranas set him up against his grandfather. This time, in June 2001, the country was in shock and grieving. He took the throne as the Maoist war grew fiercer. In October 2002 he dismissed the elected prime minister, Sher Bahadur Deuba, and began appointing governments himself.

On 1 February 2005 he took direct power. He declared a state of emergency, cut phone lines and had political leaders arrested. The parties and the Maoists began working together against him. In April 2006 weeks of mass protests, the second People's Movement, filled the streets. On 24 April he gave in and restored parliament.

In November 2006 the government and the Maoists signed a peace agreement. The war had cost about 17,000 lives. A Constituent Assembly was elected in April 2008, and at its first sitting, on 28 May 2008, it voted to abolish the monarchy. Nepal became a republic. In June Gyanendra left Narayanhiti Palace, which became a museum. He has lived on in Nepal as a private citizen.

claims.text: Gyanendra was briefly made king as a three-year-old in 1950.
claims.note: The Ranas crowned him on 7 November 1950 after Tribhuvan fled to the Indian embassy. India refused to recognise him.

claims.text: On 1 February 2005 he dismissed the government and took power himself.
claims.note: Announced in his televised address that day. The arrests and phone cuts were widely reported.
